articles.title: Nitecore’s latest power bank is the lightest and most compact yet
articles.summary: You gotta pay to play though.
articles.body: There’s two things you should know about me, your intrepid reviewer: I hate the feature creep associated with modern power banks, and I love shaving grams off the gear I carry when backpacking,  bikepacking, and trail running. So imagine my delight when Nitecore released a new generation of its ultralight NB10000 battery. After a few weeks with it I can confidently say: Haribo be damned! The $83.95 NB10000 Gen 4 weighs just 146 grams, according to my scale, and measures 1.45 x 11.6 x 4.68cm (0.57 x 4.57 x 1.84 inches), according to Nitecore’s spec sheet. That makes it the lightest and most compact 10,000mAh power bank I can find. Even when factoring in the extra 6 grams added by the included USB-C lanyard, it still beats the previous ultralight champ: Nitecore’s NB10000 Gen 3. The secret to the Gen 4’s impressive weight is a silicon-carbon anode, the same battery tech increasingly appearing in flagship smartphones, including Samsung’s. As small as it is, the Gen 4’s 39Wh battery still fully recharged my aging iPhone 15 Pro twice, with a few watt-hours left in the tank. And with up to 22.5W of output, it can even top-up my 14-inch MacBook Pro when needed. It also supports pass-through to charge your gadgets as the power bank itself charges.  Have I found power bank perfection? Almost. [Product: Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 power bank | https://www.amazon.com/Nitecore-NB10000-Gen4-Ultralight-Waterproof/dp/B0H61KHJ1X?ref_=ast_bl_cpl_dp&tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnitecorestore.com%2Fproducts%2Fnb10000gen4-usbc-lightweight-power-bank%3Fsrsltid%3DAfmBOooHNY3mDGYbFdgcud_tG1qt5Ar7j__UEylyC4YeNRFRiMwTInnm] I like that the NB10000 Gen 4 gets all the basics right. It has a simple, four-element indicator to show the battery level, which I much prefer over a fancy display. It’s constructed out of carbon fiber sheets and offers IPX7 protection against water ingress, allowing it to withstand rain or even temporary submersion – exactly what you want from an adventure battery. In my testing, I measured 33.58Wh of the claimed 39Wh capacity for an 86.1 percent efficiency. That’s a pretty good result for a premium power bank and a slight improvement on the 33.33Wh we measured on the Gen 3 model. That works out to 229.98Wh/kg of delivered energy, or 220.90Wh/kg with the cable — class-leading results, either way. The NB10000 Gen 4 supports PD, QC3.0, and Huawei’s SCP charging protocols. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG20260806183138.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_3261.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_3157.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_3305.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The Gen 4 model also didn’t suffer from the overheating and shutdown issues we saw when the Gen 3 would run low on juice. I did, however, see a temporary interruption in power delivery when the Gen 4 unit was almost fully depleted, but that’s only because I had a meter attached — otherwise I wouldn’t have known since it continued charging almost immediately.  The only thing that could be considered superfluous is the animated RGB lighting that flows around the dual USB-C ports. The lights are there to guide you to the USB-C ports in a dark tent, says Nitecore, but you can also… feel them. Give the battery a double-knock near the top and the lights (and battery indicator) illuminate. This can be helpful if wearing gloves since Nitecore inexplicably opted for a touch-sensitive wake button on the Gen 4. Fortunately, that so-called “Touch Button” did reliably sense my wet finger in testing. The knock-to-wake feature seemed to only work about 75 percent of the time, but it, and the RGB lights, can be disabled if you want. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_3211.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2788.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG20260806183232.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG20260806183224.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2813.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2803.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2941.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2771.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The lights will also glow yellow (regular mode) or green (eco) after a long press of the power button if you want to toggle between full power and extended life, respectively. Eco mode works by dropping the output to a slow 5W (5V at 1A) max. This can keep the power bank from automatically shutting off when charging low-draw devices like headlamps, watches, or wireless earbuds. It can also yield a little more total charge capacity by producing less heat waste, and allow the battery to operate closer to its native voltage resulting in less conversion loss. The Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 is the ideal power bank for endurance athletes, backpackers, or anyone looking for an ultralight and ultracompact power bank that mostly avoids feature creep. The only real negative is the price, having gone up to $83.95 since the launch of the $64.95 Gen 3 model two years ago. That makes the Gen 4 power bank two to three times more expensive than the typical 10,000mAh power bank, but it can save you 50 grams or more. That’s a price premium I can see lots of active, outdoorsy people happily paying for. All photos by Thomas Ricker / The Verge

articles.title: Taylor Farms is recalling guacamole, salsa, taco dip, and more.
articles.summary:
After health officials linked its lettuce to the nationwide Cyclospora outbreak, Taylor Farms is now recalling over a dozen products containing jalapeños across Walmart, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s, and Kroger.
These products contain fresh peppers from Coast Citrus Distributors, which recently recalled its jalapeños over Salmonella contamination. Taylor Farms says it’s not “aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.”

articles.standfirst: Missão Chang’e-7 faz parte dos esforços de Pequim para levar astronautas à Lua até 2030; lançamento foi adiado após uma avaliação das condições da operação.
articles.summary: Missão Chang’e-7 faz parte dos esforços de Pequim para levar astronautas à Lua até 2030; lançamento foi adiado após uma avaliação das condições da operação.
articles.body:
A Agência Espacial Tripulada da China anunciou neste domingo (23) o adiamento da missão de pesquisa lunar Chang’e-7 , que é parte dos esforços de Pequim para enviar astronautas à Lua até 2030. A decisão ocorre menos de duas semanas após uma falha que resultou na explosão de um foguete durante o lançamento.

Após uma “avaliação exaustiva”, a agência afirmou que a missão, que levaria a sonda Chang’e-7 ao espaço a bordo de um foguete, “não atende às condições de lançamento” e não poderá ocorrer na janela prevista para este ano.

Segundo a agência, o adiamento foi decidido com base nos princípios de “prudência, confiabilidade e sucesso absoluto da missão”. Não foram divulgados detalhes sobre quais condições não foram atendidas nem uma nova data para o lançamento.

Foguete dá ré? China consegue feito inédito ao fazer propulsor voltar e pousar em terra firme

China quer levar cães-robôs à Lua para construir base com astronautas até 2035

China lança missão para se preparar para ida à Lua; astronauta chinês passará um ano no espaço pela primeira vez

A missão, que tem como objetivo buscar água no polo sul da Lua, estava prevista para ser lançada neste fim de semana ou na próxima segunda-feira (24), segundo a imprensa chinesa.

A China destinou bilhões de dólares ao programa espacial nos últimos anos, como parte do projeto que o presidente Xi Jinping chama de “sonho espacial” do país.

Em julho, a China conseguiu pousar pela primeira vez um foguete reutilizável , segundo a agência espacial do país. O feito foi considerado uma etapa importante para o desenvolvimento do programa espacial chinês e para a redução dos custos de lançamento.

A China pretende enviar astronautas à Lua até 2030. Os Estados Unidos perseguem uma meta semelhante por meio do programa Artemis.

O foguete Zhuque-3, da empresa privada chinesa LandSpace, decola da Zona Piloto de Inovação Espacial Comercial de Dongfeng, no noroeste da China — próximo a Jiuquan, na província de Gansu —, em 19 de agosto de 2026. — Foto: cnsphoto via REUTERS

articles.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El NiÃ±o grows
articles.summary: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.body:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El NiÃ±o is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.

While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable.

Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.

The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.

What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.

El NiÃ±o brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.

El NiÃ±o is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries .

This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further.

"The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El NiÃ±o is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton.

"All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added.

The waters far away from El NiÃ±o's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.

The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.

Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas.

The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels.

"The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,â said Smyth.

Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.

Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.

The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.

articles.body: For most kids, finding a spider would be a scream, and then a quick retreat. But for Murphy Widdowson, it was a scientific discovery. What began as a routine encounter with a tiny spider on a remote Australian island eventually led experts to identify a previously unknown species, and give it a name that would forever be linked to the curious schoolboy who found it. According to a Daily Mail report from 2021, Murphy was 10 years old in 2020 and was staying on Deal Island off the northeast coast of Tasmania while his parents worked there. While on the remote island Murphy picked up a small spider that intrigued him, and he decided not to wonder what sort of spider he'd found, but to seek the opinion of an expert. Seeking help identifying his strange find, he contacted the Queen Victoria Museum and Art Gallery in Launceston. And Museum arachnologist John Douglas was unable to identify the specimen with certainty, suggesting Murphyâs find may be more than meets the eye. Scroll down to know what happened next.Mystery spider investigated by expertsAccording to Daily Mail, The specimen was then sent for further examination to spider taxonomist Dr Volker Framenau in Western Australia. The researchers, after examining the spider, determined it was a new species of wolf spider, unknown to science before. The find was significant because the spider looked very much like other members of its genus, making it hard to identify with the naked eye. Douglas said that the key differences could only be seen under a microscope. The researchers were able to establish that it was a separate species, in particular because of the spider's unusual sexual organs. The newly discovered spider was named Artoriopsis murphyi, in honor of Murphy and his curiosity that led the specimen to scientists in the first place.A tiny spider with a huge storyThe find is also a reminder of how much of Australia's diverse ecosystem remains to be documented. Douglas said although new species are discovered regularly, relatively few Australian arachnologists have the time or resources to formally describe spiders. That makes Murphyâs discovery even more remarkable. A child on a remote island saw something strange, asked questions, reached out to expertsâand contributed to the scientific record. His story demonstrates that scientific discoveries donât always begin in fancy labs. Sometimes it begins with curiosity, with the readiness to ask, âWhat is this?âA celebration worthy of a new speciesMurphyâs achievement was later celebrated with a special presentation attended by his family and teacher, museum staff and volunteers. The celebration even had a cake decorated with the spider's new scientific name, Artoriopsis murphyi. For Murphy, the discovery turned a small spider he encountered as a child into a lasting scientific legacy. His name will now go alongside the species that he drew to the attention of researchers.Should arachnophobes be afraid?Fortunately for anyone wary of spiders, Artoriopsis murphyi is not believed to be dangerous to humans. The spider is only about five millimeters in size and Douglas said that even if it did bite a person it would be unlikely to cause any noticeable sensation if it managed to pierce the skin. So Murphy's discovery may sound like an arachnophobe's nightmare, but the tiny wolf spider is much more significant scientifically than it is dangerous. Ultimately Artoriopsis murphyi is a story about curiosity, exploration and the surprises that can occur when a young person takes the time to look closely at the world around them.Images Courtesy: Daily Mail

articles.title: For 30 years, the âKerry cowâ bones were seen as proof of early farming in Ireland; scientists now say they belonged to a bear and wild boar
articles.summary: Science News: For more than three decades, a collection of animal bones from Irelandâs Ferriterâs Cove was considered some of the earliest evidence that farming had.
articles.body: For more than three decades, a collection of animal bones from Irelandâs Ferriterâs Cove was considered some of the earliest evidence that farming had reached the island. But new research has now overturned that interpretation. According to University College Dublin (UCD), bones once identified as cattle have instead been identified as belonging to a bear and wild boar. The finding challenges a long-standing understanding of Irelandâs transition from hunter-gatherer societies to farming communities. It also highlights how modern scientific techniques can reveal new information from archaeological remains that were excavated and studied decades ago.The mystery of the âKerry cowâ bonesThe bones were discovered during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriterâs Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula in County Kerry, southwestern Ireland. They were associated with the Late Mesolithic period, a time when people on the island still lived primarily as hunter-gatherers. Because they had been identified as cattle bones, archaeologists regarded them as particularly important. Domestic cattle would have indicated contact between Irelandâs Mesolithic communities and Neolithic farming societies elsewhere in Europe.For more than 30 years, the remains were therefore used as evidence that farming communities or their animals had reached Ireland before agriculture became firmly established there. The bones became informally known as the âKerry cowâ remains.Scientists take another lookThe original identification was not as certain as its long-standing importance might suggest. Researchers from University College Dublin and University College Cork recently revisited the specimens and found that their original classification was ambiguous. Instead of relying only on the physical appearance and shape of the fragments, the researchers used a modern technique called Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry, or ZooMS.The method examines proteins preserved in the collagen of ancient bones. Different animal species have distinctive protein patterns, allowing scientists to identify remains even when the bones are fragmented or lack obvious features. The team sent samples to a laboratory at Franceâs National Centre for Scientific Research in Lille for analysis. The results showed that the supposedly bovine remains actually came from a bear and wild boar. That finding removed what had been considered a crucial piece of evidence for the early arrival of domestic animals in Ireland.Why the discovery mattersThe significance of the discovery goes far beyond correcting the identity of a few old bones. For decades, archaeologists had used the supposed cattle remains to support the idea that Mesolithic hunter-gatherers in Ireland had interacted with Neolithic farming communities elsewhere in Europe before 4000 B.C.E. If the bones were not cattle, that evidence disappears.According to UCD researchers, the new findings mean there is currently no archaeological evidence that domesticated cattle, and by extension early farming communities, had reached or influenced Ireland before 4000 B.C.E. This could require archaeologists to reconsider when and how the transition from hunting and gathering to farming occurred on the island.The change is particularly important because the arrival of farming was a major transformation in European prehistory. Farming involved not only the cultivation of crops and keeping of domesticated animals, but also major changes in settlement, diet, technology and social organisation. The Irish story of that transformation now appears less straightforward than previously thought.The surprising identity of the bearThe researchers have established that at least some of the remains came from a bear, but they have not yet determined exactly which type. Scientists are carrying out further analysis to determine whether the bear remains belonged to brown bears or polar bears. This question is significant because brown bears once lived across Ireland before eventually becoming extinct there.The discovery could therefore contribute not only to archaeological research into farming but also to the study of Irelandâs ancient wildlife.A lesson from old collectionsThe story also demonstrates how modern scientific techniques can transform interpretations of archaeological discoveries made decades ago. The bones were not newly discovered. Researchers simply returned to material that had already been excavated and preserved. With technologies unavailable to the original investigators, they were able to ask new questions of the old specimens.Martin Moucheron, an archaeologist at University College Dublin who led the research, emphasised that re-examining existing archaeological material with new techniques could reveal evidence that earlier researchers were unable to recognise. The âKerry cowâ story is therefore a reminder that archaeology is not always about finding something new in the ground. Sometimes, a major discovery can come from taking a second look at something that has been sitting in a collection for decades.In this case, that second look transformed supposed cattle bones into evidence of ancient wildlife, and potentially removed one of the key pieces of evidence supporting an early connection between Irelandâs hunter-gatherers and Europeâs first farming communities.

articles.title: Vietnam Revises EPR Policy to Improve Circularity
articles.summary: The Vietnam Department of Environment’s draft policy calls for strengthening the role of private sector stakeholders in implementing EPR practices.
articles.body:
Vietnam is making moves to revise its extended producer responsibility (EPR) policy to better promote the development of a circular economy.

Announced at the "Pathways for a Robust Extended Producer Responsibility System in Vietnam " workshop in Hanoi, the revision applies to the 2020 Law on Environmental Protection and its included regulations, including provisions addressing EPR.

Mills Update: Japan, Vietnam and Indonesia Producers on How Sustainability is Evolving

Op-Ed: Doubling Down on Circular Fashion Requires More Than Regulation

Vietnam Faces Trade Squeeze as Wages Rise

Tăng The Cuong, director general of Vietnam's Department of Environment, said that EPR should not be viewed merely as a financial obligation for businesses, but rather a mechanism that incentivizes changes in product design, material selection, collection and recycling systems, and investment in circular solutions.

Cuong said that Vietnam has made significant progress in establishing and implementing EPR over the past six years, but the practice still has room for improvement. To boost transparency and effectiveness, the nation needs to offer stronger incentives for the collection and recycling market.

The Vietnam Department of Environment's draft policy calls for strengthening the role of private sector stakeholders in implementing EPR practices. The nation aims to do that by focusing on developing policies, legal frameworks and monitoring mechanisms that would require producers to directly organize collection and recycling of post-consumer products and packaging either independently or using third-party producer responsibility organization recyclers. The updated policy also will eliminate the ability for producers to simply make financial contributions to the Vietnam Environment Protection Fund as a means of fulfilling their recycling obligations.

Francesca Nardini, deputy resident representative of the United Nations Development Program in Vietnam said the next challenge for the nation will be developing an EPR system that operates effectively, sustainably and in accordance with market demands.

"EPR should not only ensure regulatory compliance or meet recycling targets, but also help transform how resources circulate within the economy, create value from materials that might otherwise become waste and encourage investment and innovation," she said.

Apparel is one of Vietnam's largest industries, valued at $7.52 billion in 2025 and growing at a compound annual growth rate of 6.80 percent to reach $11.14 billion by 2031, according to Ken Research. The country's packaging sector is heavily connected to apparel, particularly with the growth of e-commerce.

During the event in Hanoi, Dr. Fritz Flanderka, executive director of packaging specialist the Reclay Group, said there is no universal EPR model that will fit all scenarios. The core focus can be shifting recycling and collection responsibility to businesses, but the design and operation of these systems must be tailored to the markets and institutions they regulate.

With that in mind, PROs will play a central role in any EPR policy, connecting producers with collection, sorting and recycling networks. Experts at the Hanoi summit said the responsibilities of PROs, along with capacity requirements and oversight mechanisms, must be clearly defined in EPR policy. Under the policy revisions currently under consideration, PROs would be mandated to meet requirements related to organizational ability for collection, financial capacity, electronic data management and accounting.

Currently, informal waste pickers and scrap collectors make up a large portion of Vietnam's collection system, so the new policy also will factor in that labor so that workers aren't left behind. And the revision also will take into account the time constraints and investments needed to roll out a more developed EPR system, so mandatory recycling rates would be adjusted in phases to allow producers time to prepare for compliance.

articles.title: Avulux lands FDA de novo classification for light-sensitive migraine lenses
articles.summary: Avulux’s lens technology uses a optical filters to block up to 97% of blue, amber, and red light while letting soothing green light through.
articles.body:
Avulux has obtained de novo marketing authorisation from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its optical lenses for managing light sensitivity associated with migraine, making it the first product of its kind to achieve the designation.

The Florida-based company's precision optical filter is indicated to decrease the impact of light sensitivity in patients aged 12 years and older diagnosed with episodic migraine.

Research indicates that over 45 million people in the US are affected by episodic migraine, while up to 90% of people living with the neurological condition cite light sensitivity as a symptom, with up to 60% of migraine attacks triggered by harsh light or glare. Episodic migraine occurs on fewer than 15 days per month.

Worn like regular eyeglasses, Avulux's lens technology uses a dual-band optical filter that is designed to block up to 97% of blue, amber, and red light -- light wavelengths that stimulate intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (IPRGCs) and have been demonstrated to exacerbate headache-associated light sensitivity -- while letting soothing green light pass through, the company stated.

Clearance for the eyeglasses, which are intended to complement rather than replace usual migraine care such as the gold standard of triptans, was supported by Avulux's clinical evidence from several studies. In a clinical evaluation (NCT04341298), Avulux's IPRGC lenses were associated with clinically and statistically significant reductions in two- and four-hour headache pain in a post-hoc analyses of 78 patients with baseline headache pain scores ≥ 2 on an 11-point scale.

Avulux's CEO, Dr Charles Posternack, commented: "For a long time, light sensitivity was seen as just a symptom of migraine. That thinking has changed. There is growing recognition that light sensitivity is a serious medical concern in its own right.

"This authorisation gives patients and providers a clear, FDA-recognised option designed specifically to manage the impact of light in those with migraine, one we hope will soon become the standard of medical care in this population."

In the medtech industry, companies are at various developmental stages for migraine treatments that are designed to provide relief via neuromodulation. These include ShiraTronics, which is developing an implantable neuromodulation system for chronic migraine (CM) relief. In a readout from September 2025 , the company's system demonstrated an 11.3-day mean reduction in monthly headache days (MHD) for CM patients in a pilot study evaluating its device.

Meanwhile, Theranica 's neuromodulation-based therapy for relieving migraine symptoms secured FDA clearance in March 2023, and Nocira gained approval breakthrough device designation from the agency in April 2022 for its automated variable pulse insufflation (AVPI) device that administers gentle, controlled puffs of air in the ears to treat migraine attacks. However, prescription drugs such as triptans remain the go-to treatment for the condition.

"Avulux lands FDA de novo classification for light-sensitive migraine lenses" was originally created and published by Medical Device Network , a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.title: The bubbling surface of doomed supergiant star Betelgeuse has been revealed like never before
articles.summary: Betelgeuse may be a well-known and often-studied stellar object, but that doesn't mean astronomers aren't capable of capturing this doomed star in a complete...
articles.body:

Betelgeuse may be a well-known and often-studied stellar object, but that doesn't mean astronomers aren't capable of capturing this doomed star in a completely new light.

A team of scientists examined the doomed red supergiant star with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), gaining new, highly detailed insights into its turbulent surface. Betelgeuse, located around 600 light-years away, captured the public's attention a few years ago when the rapid and dramatic dimming of the infamous highly evolved star led some scientists to hypothesize that it was about to explode in a spectacular supernova . That hasn't happened, and scientists are now less convinced that this explosion is immediately imminent, but Betelgeuse remains the subject of intense scientific scrutiny.

"Its eventual fate as a supernova makes it fascinating to know what it actually looks like now," team leader Bill Dent, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory (ESO), said in a statement.

The newly released ALMA images of Betelgeuse, captured in 2023, show bright hotspots on the star's surface and an almost corrugated texture arising from vast amounts of plasma shifting through the star, which has around 20 times the mass of our sun , but is puffed out to around 800 times the size of our star.

The observations show the red supergiant has an atmosphere with a temperature of around 3,680 degrees Fahrenheit (2,030 degrees Celsius), but possesses at least two regions even hotter than this. One of these areas is 980 degrees Fahrenheit (530 degrees Celsius) hotter than the plasma surrounding it.

The uneven nature seen by ALMA is likely the result of massive convective movements in the star, hot plasma rising through the star and generating shockwaves that erupt in the star's atmosphere, creating bright and hot regions. The familiarity of Betelgeuse to astronomers doesn't mean the star isn't capable of delivering surprises too. When the team compared images collected in 2023 to observations from 2015, they were surprised to see a hotspot in the northeast of the stellar disk has persisted for at least seven years, that is much longer than predicted by current stellar models.

The orientation of the hotspots of Betelgeuse also added support to the idea that the red supergiant star is orbited by an elusive companion star .

Astronomers will continue to monitor the hotspots of Betelgeuse with ALMA to determine how fixed they are and how their evolution relates to things like mass loss, and the structure of the star's atmosphere.

That investigation will likely continue until Betelgeuse finally ends its life in a supernova explosion. The team's research has been accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics and is available on the paper repository site arXiv.

Betelgeuse, located around 600 light-years away, captured the public's attention a few years ago when the rapid and dramatic dimming of the infamous highly evolved star led some scientists to hypothesize that it was about to explode in a spectacular supernova . That hasn't happened, and scientists are now less convinced that this explosion is immediately imminent, but Betelgeuse remains the subject of intense scientific scrutiny.
"Its eventual fate as a supernova makes it fascinating to know what it actually looks like now," team leader Bill Dent, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory (ESO), said in a statement.

The newly released ALMA images of Betelgeuse, captured in 2023, show bright hotspots on the star's surface and an almost corrugated texture arising from vast amounts of plasma shifting through the star, which has around 20 times the mass of our sun , but is puffed out to around 800 times the size of our star.

The observations show the red supergiant has an atmosphere with a temperature of around 3,680 degrees Fahrenheit (2,030 degrees Celsius), but possesses at least two regions even hotter than this. One of these areas is 980 degrees Fahrenheit (530 degrees Celsius) hotter than the plasma surrounding it.

The uneven nature seen by ALMA is likely the result of massive convective movements in the star, hot plasma rising through the star and generating shockwaves that erupt in the star's atmosphere, creating bright and hot regions. The familiarity of Betelgeuse to astronomers doesn't mean the star isn't capable of delivering surprises too. When the team compared images collected in 2023 to observations from 2015, they were surprised to see a hotspot in the northeast of the stellar disk has persisted for at least seven years, that is much longer than predicted by current stellar models.
The orientation of the hotspots of Betelgeuse also added support to the idea that the red supergiant star is orbited by an elusive companion star .

Astronomers will continue to monitor the hotspots of Betelgeuse with ALMA to determine how fixed they are and how their evolution relates to things like mass loss, and the structure of the star's atmosphere.

That investigation will likely continue until Betelgeuse finally ends its life in a supernova explosion. The team's research has been accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics and is available on the paper repository site arXiv.

articles.title: Brain cells and chemical signals could hold the missing piece of memory
articles.summary: Brain cells and chemical signals could hold the missing piece of memory that today's silicon computers cannot reproduce
articles.body:

Brain chemistry may contribute to memory beyond ordinary electrical signalling

AI systems process information without the living cellular environment found inside brains

Astrocytes could play an important role in processing cognitive information

A new scientific model argues that binary code, the 0s and 1s underlying every computer, cannot fully explain how memory works.

Researchers Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem base their model on molecular and cellular evidence.

Their theory, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, proposes that three biological components, not binary switches, are what generate genuine memory.

A chemical basis for how memory actually forms

Unlike a silicon chip storing information as binary states, the tripartite model proposes that memory arises through three separate biological elements interacting.

These elements include brain cells, particularly astrocytes, interacting with neurons, along with the molecular environment surrounding those individual cells directly.

A third component involves specific chemicals, such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters, circulating continuously throughout the brain's living tissue.

The researchers suggest that living brains may do more than simply transmit electrical signals between individual neurons scattered across tissue.

They may also write and read certain kinds of information chemically, a process with no clear equivalent inside a silicon processor.

Astrocytes, abundant brain cells that interact closely with neurons, occupy a particularly important place within this newly proposed scientific model.

Marx and Gilon propose that clusters of astrocytes participate in processing cognitive information alongside neurons and the surrounding cellular environment.

A central part of their argument holds that biological memories are never simply pieces of stored logical information by themselves.

They argue that biological memory carries an emotional dimension that no binary code stored inside a computer's memory bank can replicate.

Their model treats chemical messengers, including neurotransmitters, as essential parts of the mechanism by which cognitive information becomes fully encoded.

What the chemistry of memory means for AI

Both computers and biological brains can store and retrieve information, though their underlying mechanisms may differ in fundamental ways.

In a computer, information ultimately carries a physical aspect that is encoded directly into its silicon hardware and internal circuitry.

Marx and Gilon ask whether biological memory also carries a physical aspect, though one rooted in living cells and organic chemistry.

That distinction grows increasingly relevant as AI systems become more capable of performing tasks tied closely to human logical reasoning.

Their paper directly challenges the assumption that greater computational power and complexity alone would necessarily produce biological-like consciousness in machines.

The researchers argue that purely electronic systems lack the biological infrastructure and emotional processes characteristic of living, breathing organisms entirely.

Their argument is not that AI cannot perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks as computing power keeps expanding rapidly each year.

Rather, it raises a more fundamental question about whether intelligent behaviour equals the biological processes producing memory, emotion, and thought.

articles.title: Alfalfa Sprouts Were Linked to E. Coli and Salmonella at the Same Time — Here’s How That’s Possible
articles.summary: Among the 55 cases reported in the outbreaks, at least two people were infected with both bacteria.
articles.body:
Everything Sprouts recalled select lots of Everything Sprouts and Calco alfalfa sprouts because of potential E. coli and Salmonella contamination. The outbreak has been linked to 55 illnesses across 15 states and four hospitalizations.

Alfalfa sprouts are considered a higher-risk food because the warm, moist conditions used to germinate the seeds also favor bacterial growth. Bacteria on contaminated seeds can grow during germination and become trapped within microscopic tissues, making them difficult to wash away.

Consumers should dispose of recalled sprouts and clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers they touched. Older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, and immunocompromised people should avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts.

The summer of foodborne outbreaks now includes an alfalfa sprout recall linked to two foodborne illnesses. Everything Sprouts, LLC has recalled select lots of its alfalfa sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands due to potential contamination with E. coli and Salmonella .

To date, 55 cases linked to the recall have been reported across 15 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Four people have been hospitalized in connection with the outbreak, and at least two have been infected with both E. coli and Salmonella .

"Everything Sprouts became aware of reports of illnesses from federal and state agencies," the company said in a statement . "During this outbreak, we have tested our products daily and have not received any positive lab results. We continue to work closely with public health officials to investigate the source of this potential issue and will provide updates as they become available."

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) maintains the full list of recalled products, including lot numbers and bar codes.

The recall is raising many questions about how you can get two illnesses from one food. As you can imagine, "it has been very rare to have more than one bacterial pathogen causing outbreaks and recalls in the past," says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez , PhD, director of the Center for Food Safety at the University of Georgia. But alfalfa sprouts have unique characteristics that make them ideal breeding grounds for bacteria — even two types at once, according to Kalmia E. Kniel , PhD, professor and chair of microbial food safety at the University of Delaware.

How can alfalfa sprouts be contaminated with two types of bacterial pathogens at once?

"Sprouts are often considered higher-risk products," Kniel says. The seeds are germinated to create sprouts in moist, humid, warm environments, and these are the same conditions that favor the growth of bacteria, including Salmonella and E. coli , she explains. It's usually thought that the fields where the alfalfa seeds were grown could have been contaminated by irrigation or runoff water, soil, or animal waste, Diez-Gonzalez says.

"There is often concern that the seeds are contaminated," Kniel says. As a result, the seeds are often soaked in chlorinated water . "But soaking the seeds in chlorinated water will not completely inactivate the pathogens, as the bacteria are protected in the crevices of the seeds," Kniel says.

Related: Recalls Are Rising: This Is How Food Safety Experts Decide What's Safe to Eat

Multiple alfalfa sprout recalls have been linked to E. coli or Salmonella separately, Diez-Gonzalez says. "According to most of the evidence, the bacteria can be present in the seeds after contamination of the fields where the alfalfa plants are grown as a source of seeds," he says. But when the seeds are germinated, the bacteria can grow into the sprouts.

At that point, "bacteria present on the seed shell can become trapped within microscopic tissues, making them impossible to wash away," Kniel says. "These aren't two separate contamination events," says Amesh A. Adalja , MD, an infectious disease expert and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "The seed is the shared vehicle."

What are the symptoms of an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection?

It depends. "These bacteria attach to different receptors, provoke different inflammatory responses," Adalja says.

These illnesses can look "indistinguishable without testing," according to Adalja. However, he says that someone with an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection would likely experience cramps, diarrhea, fever, and sometimes bloody stool, given the "overlap" in symptoms between E. coli and Salmonella infections.

Related: The Food Recall System Is Broken, and Experts Say We're All at Risk

Doctors would typically only know if you have two infections if you're given a multiplex PCR gastrointestinal panel that tests your stool sample against several potential pathogens, Adalja explains.

While these co-infections aren't common, Adalja says they may have occurred in the past more often than people realize. "Co-infections almost certainly occurred in earlier sprout outbreaks, but clinicians weren't using tools in a way that would find them," he says.

When did the E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks start?

Illnesses linked to the outbreak began on May 31 and have continued since then, according to the CDC .

According to the CDC, 76% of the 34 interviewed patients said they'd eaten alfalfa sprouts before getting sick. Epidemiological evidence and traceback information from restaurants and grocery stores suggest that Everything Sprouts could be fueling the outbreak.

What should you do if you have recalled alfalfa sprouts?

If you have the recalled products at home, the FDA and CDC recommend disposing of them. Then, clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers the sprouts may have touched.

Alfalfa sprouts remain a high-risk food regardless of whether there is a recall, Kniel points out. "Vulnerable populations — older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, and anyone immunocompromised — should avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts," she says.

If you really love alfalfa sprouts but want to lower your risk of getting sick under ordinary circumstances, Diez-Gonzalez suggests cooking your sprouts before eating them.

Fast Facts: Alfalfa sprouts linked to E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks

Which alfalfa sprout products are being recalled? These products have been recalled as part of the outbreak, according to the FDA :

Everything Sprouts and Calco-branded alfalfa sprouts (5 ounces) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, or 230 and bar codes 860014523113, 860014523120, or 850079470149

Everything Sprouts Crunchy Protein Sprout Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 226, and 230

Everything Sprouts Zesty Garlic Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, and 230

Where have illnesses linked to the recalled sprouts been reported? Infections have been detected in these states, according to the CDC : Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Washington, and Wisconsin

articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from £3m fund

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.

That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.

Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.

For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.
RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.
It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.
While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.
The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."
Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.
The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.
It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.
Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.
But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.
Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.
He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.
He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.
That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.
Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.
If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.
Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.
But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.
For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.
